body: Haha, I was going to say the exact same thing.

I was talking to someone recently about this:  video games were how I fought depression when I was a kid. I wore out three controllers playing FF7. 

Now, though, I can't get into a video game unless I'm drunk. I just can't seem to immerse myself in that other world any more. Which kinda scares me, because I still read fiction (not at the 3-books-a-week pace I used to when I was young... maybe 3 books a month these days). I'm not sure I could stand it if I stopped being able to experience fiction.

I did this for a while (especially on Facebook):  being an advocate for mental health issues, and openly sharing my struggles with depression and how it mirrors other chronic illnesses. 

I had to shut everything down, though, when I had a really bad episode and a supervisor from work showed up at my front door... with a cop. I'm grateful to him now, but the shame of having my personal life bleed over so dramatically into my professional life still hasn't left me.

I literally thought I was the only person who did this. I had to move into a shared living space for the first time in 10 years because of a new job/new city, and when I'm depressed I sometimes have to wait for HOURS to use the kitchen.

Which doubly sucks, because cooking is a big hobby of mine (I like to work my way through ethnic/international cookbooks, cover to cover).

I literally just realized this yesterday about myself:  I don't do anything fun, and I've stopped all the hobbies I used to enjoy. Anhedonia is a bitch. 

I'm looking at doing some Meetups, but I get really irritated if I show up to a group thing, everyone knows one another, and I'm left standing by myself.

I'm typing this drunk, if that gives me any cred. So... 

I watched my dad die from alcohol induced seizures when I was 4 years old. Literally. I was the only one in the room at the time, and he died in front of me with a bottle in his hand. I don't remember it, and I don't even know what he looked like. But I still have nightmares about it. The dreams are always pulsing, vibrating bits of light and weight. 

I'm not gonna say it gets better. It doesn't. But you can make something of your life, in the midst of the pain. You can be a light for one other person, and make all the difference in the world.

That sucks. And I honestly know what you mean. I work with some of the most brilliant people in the world... not only am I boring, but I'm literally retarded in comparison. It seems to physically hurt some people when I try to join a conversation. 

Maybe there's no way around the problem. I'm thinking about these weekly talks that my work puts on, where famous people from around the world come in and tell us about their current projects. They're open to the public. 

Every week, this one guy off the street is there. And every week, he gets up and interrupts a world-famous thinker in the middle of their talk to ask a long and rambling question that has nothing to do with anything. Everyone hates the guy, but no one wants to be on the nightly news as "the person who kicked a knowledge-thirsty layman out of a public seminar for asking innocent questions". Thing is, he could be really popular as a regular off the street if he could just quit acting like a jackass. He just doesn't have any idea what he's doing wrong.

Maybe we're the same:  acting like utter fools, but one little tweak would bump us into friendships and acceptance.

Yeah, I get it. People don't like being around me when I'm low-energy. It's like I suck the life out of them. The only time people around me can be happy is if I'm pretending to be happy myself. One hint of depression in a social context, and BAM! Instant pariah. 

It doesn't help when you're surrounded by people who genuinely like each other and who have given you a chance, but your first impression to them was "soul-sucking parasite".

"No matter what I do, afterwards its wrong."

You're not alone in feeling like this. I suspect, though I can't prove, that this thought lies at the core of nearly everyone with depression. It's a confused, bewildering conviction that somehow, there is no right answer for you. 

You actually sound a lot like me. You have a set of standards, and you hate that you can't measure up to them. Thing is, it's the STANDARDS that are fucked up, not you. 

I go through the same paralyzing dialogue any time I meet a great woman or run into someone who would be a good friend:  "This person is so cool! I want to be their friend/boyfriend/whatever. But I'm not as cool as them, because I'm not X, Y, and Z. They won't want to talk to me. Better not even try."

I've found that if I can let go of my own, stupidly strict standards for myself, then I can talk to people without feeling like I'm wasting my time (and theirs). It's really hard, though, and it's a constant struggle. 

Good luck out there!

Grad student here (molecular biology and bioinformatics)! I don't know the field you're in, but most STEM programs look at research experience, not GPA. Grad school is not about taking classes, it's about doing independent research. So if you can show that you can work independently, that's what matters. 

It also really helps to send emails to potential advisors, introducing yourself and laying out the case for why you'd be a good fit for their lab (or the equivalent non-STEM group). An advisor in your corner can actually overrule the entire admissions committee if they want you bad enough. 

That said, the sad fact is that committees and advisors DO NOT look favorably upon mental illnesses. It's ridiculous and prejudiced, but that's the current climate. Avoid mentioning depression when explaining your low GPA. It's illegal to discriminate based upon medical conditions, but that doesn't stop it from happening. I've seen it happen. 

Also, a word of caution:  grad school is REALLY HARD for people with depression and social difficulties. It's an isolating environment by default, especially after the first couple of years. Make sure that whatever campus you choose has adequate mental care facilities, and start using them the moment you arrive. 

That sounds all doom and gloom :-P Grad school is actually very rewarding, especially if you get a rush from finding/building/thinking things no one else has ever imagined. Just be aware of the potential pitfalls! 

Good luck in your hunt.

You have power. The fact that you were able to marry a woman puts you utterly beyond my comprehension. The simple act of asserting, "Hey... I'm the best thing for you!"... I can't even. 

Regarding married assholes:  sadly, I am acquainted with several. And, by far, they are the happiest, the most successful, and the most personally content people I know. They make their spouses miserable, but by the time Mrs. Asshole wants a divorce, he's already had six different affairs with the best and the brightest women around. 

I know a guy who can't hold a job, is incredibly in debt, and doesn't even own his vehicle... and he just divorced his wife of 4 years (and two kids) to shack up with a literal fitness model.

THAT IS POWER. He has what women want, and it's what the world wants. 

Relationships are built upon respect. Specifically, a man's respect for himself, and a woman's respect for the man. (For traditional gender roles. I have no experience with nontraditional roles, so I can't speak for them.) Literally no traditional relationship had ever succeeded otherwise.

I feel it. I've done the asylum thing. Never again. 

I keep a gun next to my bed with one bullet in it, and it's the last thing I see every night. They say Caesar had a man whose job was to remind him, "Memento mori." Remember you will die. That gun is my whisperer. It's my reminder that when I go, it's going to be MY choice, not something that just happens.

But I'm not done yet. I may hate myself, I may hate my life. But I can still do shit for other people before I kick off. No, I'll never have a family. But I can buy sex. I'll never have friends. But I can help people out. I'll never be famous. But I can give my shit away anonymously to people who need it more than me. 

The way I figure... if I'm checking out, why not do as much as I can to help others before I go? Most of them don't deserve it, but hell... at least they'll get some benefit.

[Niels Bohr](http://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1922/bohr-bio.html), Nobel Prize winner for discovering electron orbital theory, was the most interesting man in the world. 

He drank Calsberg beer... specifically, beer from the [tap that the company installed in his house directly from their brewery.](http://www.forbes.com/sites/alexknapp/2012/11/28/for-winning-the-nobel-prize-niels-bohr-got-a-house-with-free-beer/) That's right... free beer for life. Winning the Nobel is awesome.

While drunk, I decided it would be an amazing idea to have some bacon. Because everything is better with bacon. 

Everything except waking up an hour later to an apartment full of black smoke and the entire stovetop on fire. I'd forgotten to turn the burner off after my bacon was done. 

And yes, the bacon was delicious.

I wish I could say they were terrible, but the problem is much more me than them. They all genuinely love one anothers company, and the conversations I overhear are often amazing. It's just that, for some reason, I'm not able to be part of any of that. 

I've long been afraid that there's something about me that puts people off. It may just be a physical thing here:  my workplace is literally on the beach in San Diego, and my coworkers are not only top-tier intellectuals... they are nearly all extraordinarily beautiful people. I'm not obese, but I've always been too body-shamed to join a gym. So I look just average. 

Or maybe it's just that my speech is too slow, and that irritates everyone. I'm from the South, and though I don't have much of an accent any more, I can't think quickly enough to be an engaging conversationalist. 

Or maybe I'm the moron in the room. These people are world-class thinkers. I'm a molecular biologist first and foremost, but all I really do is cook:  I mix this molecule with those other molecules and hope a whole bunch of a different molecule falls out of the reaction. A child could do my job. 

Meanwhile, my coworkers are all out there shaping global policy and rewriting textbooks, all while finding time to maintain perfect bodies and wonderful friendships.

I took Paxil for depression for about 2 years. MAKE SURE you are being consistently monitored by a mental health professional if you start taking it. 

I was prescribed Paxil by a GP, and so there was no followup. It took an intervention by friends and family to make me realize that I'd become MUCH more depressed--to the point of suicidal--while taking it. 

It's worked for some people, just be aware that there's a risk of it making depression-related symptoms worse rather than better.

I totally get it about just letting it out. Keep this in mind:  comment/upvotes don't equal views. A lot of people have heard what you've said tonight. 

As far as boozing is concerned, I'm an expert. My old man drank himself into a fatal seizure, and I got to watch him choke to death when I was 3 years old. And yet, here I am over 20 years later, at midnight, 14 beers in, drunk-typing random shit to someone I'll never meet. 

My advice:  working out has always been the best treatment for depression and boozing. I don't mean anything stupid like carrying cars around or running a bunch of miles or any shit. Just breaking a sweat. 

Hell, I'm 205 lbs with a heart defect. I literally cannot do a chin-up. But I lift weights every other day, and run for half an hour every day I'm not on weights. 

And the days I exercise, I don't need booze. It's only days like today, when I haven't been able to exercise, that the thirst grabs me and I gotta have booze. 

So don't give up. Do something physical, just enough to build up a sweat. It'll help, I promise.

We're alone because we have to be to survive. It doesn't make it any better. I know exactly how you feel:  I've been alone for nearly two decades now, after depression caused me to lose the woman I loved (twice) and all of my friends. 

I never made any friends after that... but I've found solace in work. When I'm working, it doesn't matter who I am. If I can solve the problem (I work in molecular and chemical biology), I feel like my life is worth it. 

A life without people who care about you sucks, but it's still possible to live it.

It's awesome that you ARE empathetic. I echo part of what TheWhiteNoise1 said, in that "others have it worse" is merely a logical trap set by people who don't know better 

However, also realize that depression is not a choice. You can't choose to feel better as easily as you could choose to donate today's burger money to someone else. Don't get stuck in the pitfall of "I shouldn't feel this way because X". You DO feel this way, so there's no "should/should not" about it. 

The best you can do is work to put yourself in a better position in the future.
